title: Never Adjust Your Steering Wheel Like This
hook: Stop setting your steering wheel height using your wrist.

script.narration: Stop setting your steering wheel height using your wrist. Most drivers learn to hold the top of the steering wheel and adjust the column until their wrist rests on top. But this common habit actually puts you at severe risk during airbag deployment and blocks your view of the instrument cluster. Today, you are going to learn the proper ergonomic way to position your steering wheel for maximum control and safety, and the most important adjustment is saved for right before the end. When you first bought your car or rented one on a trip, you probably just pulled the lever under the dash and moved the wheel until it felt somewhat comfortable. But that casual adjustment affects everything from how fast your shoulders fatigue on a long highway drive to how well you can see your speed and warning lights. Getting this right takes less than a minute, and it completely changes how connected you feel to the road. Let us break down the exact steps to find your ideal driving position without relying on outdated shortcuts.

script.narration: For generations, driving instructors taught a very specific trick. They told you to extend your arm fully and rest your wrist right on top of the steering wheel. The idea was to adjust your seat until your arm was completely straight. Millions of us learned this as the golden rule of driving posture. But here is why that old habit is actually a trap. When you stretch your arm out just to let your wrist touch the rim, it usually forces your seat way too close, or pulls the steering wheel into an awkward angle. This leaves your elbows locked and your shoulders tense, which makes smooth steering much harder when you need to react quickly. It feels natural because we were all taught it, but modern cars are built completely differently now. So if the wrist trick is outdated, what should you actually be looking for instead? The answer comes down to a vital safety space you are probably ignoring right now.

If you sit too close or angle the wheel directly at your face, an airbag deployment can force your hands backward into your own head or cause severe arm fractures. The proper steering wheel angle should point directly at your chest, not your face or your neck. This ensures the airbag deploys upward against your torso and chest cavity rather than punching straight into your jaw. If you're learning something, subscribe, it helps a lot. But the next detail about your shoulder position surprises most drivers.

Instead of checking your wrist, focus entirely on your shoulders and elbows. When your hands are placed at the nine and three o'clock positions, your elbows should have a comfortable, slight bend, never completely locked out or cramped up tight. Your back should remain firmly against the seat backrest without ever stretching, slouching, or leaning forward to reach the rim. Here is a simple test you can try right now in your driveway: turn the wheel fully to one side. If your shoulders pull away from the seat backrest when you make that turn, your steering column is adjusted completely too far away from your body. You want your upper body supported by the seat at all times so you maintain total control during sudden maneuvers. But fixing your shoulders is only half the battle, because if your wheel is blocking this one vital dashboard display, you are driving completely blind.

script.narration: Another major issue with improper steering wheel height is blocked visibility. Many drivers adjust the wheel so high that the top rim cuts right across their speedometer and warning lights. If you cannot see your fuel gauge or warning indicators without ducking your head, your wheel is set incorrectly. You should see the entire instrument panel clearly through the top half of the steering wheel opening, without any part of the rim getting in the way of your gauges. Having a clear view of your dashboard is just as important as seeing the road ahead, because missing a flashing warning light can lead to unexpected engine trouble miles down the road. But even if your dashboard is fully visible, there is one final adjustment most people completely mess up that changes everything.

Now for the final step that ties everything together. Before you even touch the steering wheel tilt lever, your seat height must be set first. Always adjust your seat cushion height so your thighs are fully supported and your feet comfortably reach the pedals with a slight bend in your knees. Only after your seat is locked in position should you adjust the steering wheel tilt and telescopic reach. Doing it in reverse order ruins your entire driving posture and forces you to hunch forward just to reach the controls. Take thirty seconds to reset your seat and wheel today, and you will immediately notice less fatigue on long drives. But wait, what about the hidden lever on the side of your seat that almost everyone uses completely wrong? Let's find out.

To recap, let us leave behind the old wrist measurement trick for good. Instead, make sure your steering wheel points directly toward your chest rather than your face, and always keep a comfortable, slight bend in your elbows while your hands rest at the nine and three o'clock positions. Remember to set your seat height and backrest angle before making your final adjustments to the steering column. Let me ask you one quick question for the comments below: do you usually prefer your steering wheel pulled all the way out toward you, or pushed further into the dash? Drop your answer down there, and before you head out, make sure to watch our other driving tip videos right here on the channel to keep improving your daily commute and stay safe on every single drive.
